name: Reactive Matter
tagline: Reactive intermediates, radical chemistry, and high-energy transformations.
seo_title: Reactive Matter — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Reactive Matter on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in radicals, carbocations, carbenes, strained molecules and reactive intermediates.

definition.lead: Reactive Matter covers the short-lived, high-energy species that chemistry runs on: radicals, carbocations, carbanions and carbenes.
definition.body: Most reactions pass through intermediates that live for microseconds or less. Learning to generate, observe and tame them has given chemists new ways to build bonds, from radical polymerization to photoredox and electrochemical synthesis.

facts.label: unpaired electron is all it takes to make a radical
Moses Gomberg discovers the first persistent organic radical, triphenylmethyl
Nobel Prize to George Olah for carbocation chemistry

branches.name: Carbenes
branches.summary: Neutral carbon with only two bonds and two non-bonding electrons.
branches.example: Stable N-heterocyclic carbenes used as ligands.

branches.name: Radical polymerization
branches.summary: Chains grown one radical addition at a time.

branches.name: Strained molecules
branches.summary: Molecules whose bond angles store energy.
branches.example: Cubane, with carbons at the corners of a cube.

branches.name: Photoredox & electrochemical radicals
branches.summary: Using light or electrodes to make radicals under mild conditions.

branches.name: Atmospheric radicals
branches.summary: Radicals that clean and change the air.
branches.example: The hydroxyl radical oxidizes many pollutants.

timeline.title: The first persistent radical
timeline.text: Moses Gomberg prepares triphenylmethyl, a carbon radical stable in solution.

timeline.title: Short-lived radicals detected
timeline.text: Friedrich Paneth and Wilhelm Hofeditz detect methyl radicals in the gas phase.
timeline.why: Showed simple radicals form during reactions.

timeline.title: The peroxide effect
timeline.text: Morris Kharasch and Frank Mayo explain anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr through radicals.
timeline.why: Radical chains became a tool for synthesis.

timeline.title: Carbocations made visible
timeline.text: George Olah observes stable carbocations by NMR in superacid solutions.
timeline.why: Turned a hypothetical intermediate into something you can study.

timeline.title: Cubane
timeline.text: Philip Eaton and Thomas Cole synthesize cubane.
timeline.why: A molecule once thought too strained to exist.

timeline.title: A bottleable carbene
timeline.text: Anthony Arduengo isolates a stable N-heterocyclic carbene.
timeline.why: Carbenes became everyday ligands and catalysts.

timeline.title: Nobel Prize for carbocations
timeline.text: George Olah receives the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

timeline.title: Controlled radical polymerization
timeline.text: Atom transfer radical polymerization is reported by Krzysztof Matyjaszewski and Mitsuo Sawamoto.

timeline.title: Metal carbenes at work
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Chauvin, Grubbs and Schrock for olefin metathesis.

timeline.title: The photoredox revival
timeline.text: David MacMillan's group couples visible-light photoredox catalysis with organocatalysis.
timeline.why: Radicals made gently with visible light became mainstream.

quiz.explain: The unpaired electron makes radicals highly reactive.

quiz.q: Which radical did Gomberg prepare in 1900?
quiz.explain: Three bulky phenyl rings protect and stabilize the radical centre.

quiz.q: Why are tertiary carbocations more stable than primary ones?
options: Alkyl groups donate electron density through hyperconjugation
They are larger, so the charge is diluted
They have more hydrogens to share the charge
They carry a negative charge as well
quiz.explain: Each neighbouring C–H or C–C bond helps share the positive charge.

options: A carbon with two bonds and two non-bonding electrons
A carbon with five bonds and no lone pair
A carbon in a triple bond to another carbon
A carbon that is always positively charged
quiz.explain: Neutral but electron-deficient, and usually very reactive.

quiz.q: Radical chlorination of methane is started by…
options: Light or heat splitting Cl₂ into chlorine atoms
Water that splits into hydroxyl radicals
A magnet that aligns the electrons
quiz.explain: Then a chain of propagation steps takes over.

quiz.q: George Olah's Nobel Prize was for…

options: An acid stronger than 100% sulfuric acid
A strong base used to remove protons
A neutral salt that conducts electricity
A weak acid used in food
quiz.explain: Strong enough to protonate even hydrocarbons.

quiz.q: The carbon of a Grignard reagent behaves as…
quiz.explain: The C–Mg bond is polarized toward carbon.

quiz.q: With peroxides, HBr adds to alkenes 'anti-Markovnikov' through…
quiz.explain: The bromine atom adds first to give the more stable carbon radical.
A ruthenium=carbon double bond swaps partners with alkenes.

options: Its carbons sit at the corners of a cube, with strained 90° angles
It is a gas that liquefies at room temperature
It is an ionic salt of carbon

quiz.q: The hydroxyl radical in the atmosphere…
options: Oxidizes many pollutants, earning it the name 'detergent of the atmosphere'
Causes rain by forming water droplets
Is mainly a greenhouse gas that traps heat
Lasts for years and builds up over time
quiz.explain: It lives for less than a second but removes methane, CO and many other gases.
